results.answerFinding: Rearrange to y=−2x/3−4/3, so m=−2/3. The inclination is the second-quadrant solution of tan θ=−2/3: θ=180°−arctan(2/3)≈146.31°. D (146°) is closest; 34°, 56° and 124° are not.
results.taughtScopeFinding: Page 62 relates straight-line gradient to the tangent of inclination; negative gradients and quadrant selection use the retained angle and sign teaching with ordinary rearrangement.
results.minimumFinding: Retain as a distinct representative: the saved straight-line item works forward from a marked inclination to slope, whereas this independently requires rearrangement and the inverse direction to an obtuse inclination.
results.difficultyReason: Rearrange a line equation for its gradient, invert the tangent and select the obtuse inclination.
corrections: Replace angle-inclination-gradient with gradient-as-tan-inclination as primary: the former taxonomy entry is for a tangent gradient in differentiation, while this is a straight line. Add rearrange-to-gradient-intercept as secondary.

results.answerFinding: For every real x, f(−x)=cos(sin(−x))=cos(−sin x)=cos(sin x)=f(x). Thus B is even. f(0)=1 rules out oddness; evenness rules out C, and the composition of continuous sine and cosine rules out D. Both answer editions agree.
results.taughtScopeFinding: Page 51 gives sine odd and cosine even identities. Applying both to a composition uses ordinary function substitution and requires no additional trigonometric method.
results.minimumFinding: Retain as a distinct representative: composition of odd and even identities is not represented by the six saved and three sealed tasks.
results.difficultyReason: Substitute a negative input into a nested function and apply both sine oddness and cosine evenness in the correct order.

results.sourceFinding: The complete source expression, domain/range choices and worked result are retained, with the exam mark intentionally omitted. The source leaves the angle unit unmarked and the native text preserves that.
results.answerFinding: The real square root exists exactly when x−2≥0, so x≥2. Put u=√(x−2); u ranges over all nonnegative values. Since −1≤sin u≤1, 0≤sin²u≤1; 0 and 1 and every intermediate value are attained as u traverses a suitable initial quarter-cycle. Thus D alone gives both the correct domain and range; A and C have the wrong domain, and B has the wrong range. Short and worked answers agree.
results.taughtScopeFinding: The supplied unit-circle and sine graph establish the bounded trigonometric values; the square-root restriction and squaring a bounded real quantity are ordinary prior algebra and function-domain transfer. No essential untaught method or invented unit convention is needed.
results.minimumFinding: Retain as a distinct representative: determining a composite function’s natural domain and a squared trigonometric range is not covered by the saved or sealed representatives.
results.difficultyReason: Combine the inner square-root restriction with the range of a squared sine and select the option satisfying both.

results.sourceFinding: The complete source expression, explicit 30° angle and all four options are retained; the mark is intentionally omitted. Short and worked answers agree with the source.
results.answerFinding: Let u=cos(2x+30°), so −1≤u≤1. Then u(1−u)=1/4−(u−1/2)²≤1/4. Equality is attainable because u=1/2 occurs, for example, at x=15°; hence A is the unique correct option and B, C and D are too large.
results.taughtScopeFinding: The unit-circle and cosine graph establish the range and attainability of 1/2; the retained quadratic-trigonometric exercise already uses algebra in a trig expression. Substitution and completing the square are ordinary prior quadratic algebra, not an essential new trigonometric method.
results.minimumFinding: Retain as a distinct representative: finding a maximum by reframing a trigonometric expression as a bounded quadratic is not represented by the saved or sealed exam tasks.
results.difficultyReason: Recognise a repeated cosine as one bounded variable, complete the square and check that the quadratic vertex is attainable.
